look_here_first: Look DOWN at the basal ROSETTE before checking flowers. Mature S. lyrata leaves are LYRATE: a larger rounded TERMINAL lobe toward the leaf tip and smaller paired LATERAL lobes closer to the stalk; some leaves vary from shallow to deeply cut. A mostly leafless square flowering stalk rises well above, bearing SMALL lavender-blue bilabiate flowers in widely spaced tiers. Cedar sage also forms a rosette, but often has separate 1–3 leaflets with long petioles and CRIMSON corollas. Do not rely on basal rosette alone.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: flowering stems rise well above rosette

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: small blue-lavender bilabiate flowers in spaced verticils

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: often in low moist/open woods, meadows, disturbed ground

key_traits.label: Basal leaf structure
key_traits.text: Lyrate/pinnatifid basal leaves: broad rounded end (terminal) lobe and smaller side lobes, often separated by narrow sinus; leaf remains ONE continuous blade, not several detached leaflets.

key_traits.label: Flowering axis
key_traits.text: Usually mostly leafless above rosette, tall unbranched or sparsely branched square stem with spaced verticils of pale blue/lavender two-lipped flowers.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Herbaceous perennial with flat basal rosette, unlike woody branching greggii/ballotiflora; green or purplish winter rosettes may persist.

key_traits.label: Lookalike cedar
key_traits.text: Cedar sage also low rosette, but broad petiolate leaves can be 1–3 FOLIOLATE (separate lateral leaflets), and crimson flowers in woodland shade; lyreleaf has a lyrately LOBED single blade and pale blue flowers. Leaf shape/calyx support identification.

key_traits.label: Leaf variation
key_traits.text: Entire to shallowly lobed leaves and purple-stained cultivated forms occur; don't claim every plant has deeply cut lobes.
